title: Bilibili：从游戏到超级平台

Bilibili: From Games to Mega-Platform
Skip to content
Weekly Digest
Bilibili: From Games to Mega-Platform
By Mark Ma •   November 1, 2026
Bilibili was founded in 2009 with anime, comics, and games (or ACG) at its core, as a danmaku video community in which viewer comments scroll across the video. Around 2020, it pushed beyond its fandom roots and leaned into other major content sections (like lifestyle, knowledge, cars). Now, as of the second quarter of 2026, Bilibili had
117M daily active users
(and 371M monthly active users) who spent an average of 113 minutes on the app each day.
When Bilibili listed on Nasdaq in 2018, games made up 71% of its revenue, and its
filings
show most of that came from one licensed Japanese mobile game,
Fate/Grand Order
. Since then, its other businesses have grown much faster, and in 2025 games made up just 21% of revenue.
Bilibili’s game revenue grew from RMB 2.94B (~$440M) in 2018 to RMB 6.39B (~$950M) in 2025. This makes it a globally underdiscussed gaming company, but this segment also pales in comparison to its growth in other areas, like its ads revenue (up from RMB 460M (~$69M) in 2018 to RMB 10.06B (~$1.5B) in 2025) and value-added services (VAS), such as memberships and livestreaming (up from RMB 590M (~$88M) to RMB 11.93B (~$1.8B)), with each segment growing roughly twentyfold.
Bilibili’s net revenue by segment, 2018–2025 | Source: Bilibili earnings releases
Today, developers and publishers promote their upcoming games on Bilibili, from big domestic single-player titles to multi-platform shooters and wuxia online games from Tencent and NetEase. For example, when a 13-minute gameplay demo for the action RPG Black Myth: Wukong was shared in 2020, the clip went on to receive more than 65M views on Bilibili. That means Bilibili reaps adjacent revenue from games that spend their publishing dollars elsewhere.
Game Science’s Black Myth account on Bilibili | Source: Bilibili
Bilibili has become a core marketing channel for games in China, yet its own game business lags far behind that influence. That makes it a useful case study. In China, game value is shifting away from the right to publish a game and toward where players decide what to play. Let’s explore how Bilibili got here, why its gaming ambitions have fallen behind, why influencing demand has become a bigger business, and what it means for the future.
Why the Original Game Model Stopped Working
In its early gaming days, Bilibili mostly published anime-style mobile games, many based on popular Japanese IP it had licensed. It could cheaply market those games to fans who already followed those series on its site. Bilibili’s biggest title was the gacha-style mobile RPG
Fate/Grand Order
(FGO), which Bilibili released in China in September 2016. Bilibili followed that with the naval-warfare collection game Azur Lane (May 2017) and the anime RPG
Princess Connect! Re:Dive
(April 2020).
Those days are long gone. When miHoYo’s anime-flavored gacha RPG
Genshin Impact
launched in September 2020, it raised the bar for quality and budgets in Chinese anime-style games, and China-developed originals (like
Genshin Impact
and
Arknights
) rose to the top of domestic revenue charts.
Sensor Tower
data shows that the combined estimated China iOS net revenue of Bilibili’s three main titles dropped 46% in the 12 months after
Genshin Impact
launched. Sensor Tower tracks in-app purchases through app stores and does not cover China’s Android channels, so these figures show trends only.
China iOS net revenue for Bilibili’s three licensed anime games, 2018–2026 | Source:
Sensor Tower
Bilibili’s two Japanese-licensed games fell hardest. In the 12 months after
Genshin Impact’s
release,
Sensor Tower
estimated that
FGO
and
Princess Connect’s
China iOS net revenue fell by 42% and 66%, respectively.
Azur Lane
, developed by a Chinese team, fared better: its revenue fell only 9%, and it hit a new high in China in 2022.
The core challenge extended beyond Japanese titles losing ground to domestic releases. Because foreign developers
cannot directly secure a Chinese gaming license
, they must team up with a local publisher — creating the exact opportunity where Bilibili once added value. Conversely, domestic studios like miHoYo and Hypergryph self-publish and don’t need a local publishing partner. As the market pivoted toward native Chinese titles, Bilibili’s primary competitive advantage diminished. Additionally, it couldn’t offset this loss solely through distribution: native games target broad multi-platform releases, making Bilibili’s
Genshin Impact
channel server just one option among many and yielding significantly lower returns than exclusive licensing deals like
FGO
.
Today, Bilibili’s platform and its games have diverged. Bilibili’s newer users came for lifestyle, knowledge, and car content, not anime-style mobile games; however, its gaming focus has largely remained with its original ACG-oriented audience.
Why Bilibili Became a Key Marketing Channel for Games
Broadening the platform didn’t bring new players to Bilibili’s own anime-style games, but it made Bilibili a place to promote all kinds of games. The platform is full of gaming creators, known as UP主, who make gameplay footage, walkthrough guides, memes, fan works, and other content about almost any game, keeping a game in conversation long after launch. That reach is a business in itself: management has said on earnings calls that
games are its top advertising sector
, without elaborating on the exact percentage.
Overseas games without a Chinese license show how this works. They cannot be sold in Chinese app stores, but Chinese players can buy them directly on Steam. For example, Netmarble’s
Solo Leveling: ARISE OVERDRIVE
is an action RPG sold only on Steam and Xbox PC. Its Bilibili account has around 3,200 followers, yet its six videos have tallied 6.5M views. The four most-watched videos align with the moments that drive purchases: pre-order openings, the launch coun
